segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: African cinema in the 1970s and 1980s witnessed an explosion of invention and creativity that rivaled any other cinematic renaissance the world has seen before or since. Directors were energized by the opportunities, the energy and the politics of the postcolonial era to create increasingly singular and ambitious films. Yet, compared with the films of the French New Wave, they seem underrated today.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Often referred to as "the father of African film," Senegalese writer and director Ousmane Sembène (1923-2007) embodied the new urgency of postcolonial Africa. In 1947, Sembène moved to France, where he worked as a docker in Marseille, joined the Communist Party and became a militant trade unionist. His cinema showed the same political and social engagement he embraced in his life, and his inspired debut came with La noire de... (Black Girl, 1966), the first feature by a Black African to gain international recognition.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Unique among the emerging directors of the 1970s was Senegal's Djibril Diop Mambéty (1945-1998), whose debut feature, Touki Bouki (1973), captured the voice of African youth and brought a dazzling, experimental touch to African cinema. Writer Manthia Diawara wrote that it "tears through the screen with fantasies of African modernity as never seen before in cinema," and critic Mark Cousins described it as "the African equivalent of Easy Rider (1969) or À bout de souffle (Breathless, 1960)." The film also has a political edge, following a young couple who dream of leaving Senegal and embark on a series of adventures to get the money they need, but who decide, at the last minute, that they cannot leave their homeland.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Inspired by the example of Sembene and also by the creation of two major African film festivals - Carthage, in Tunisia, in 1966, and Fespaco (the Panafrican Film and Television Festival), in Burkina Faso, in 1969 - there was a palpable sense of promise surrounding African cinema at the dawn of the 1970s. Electrified by writers such as Frantz Fanon, who argued in The Wretched of the Earth that national liberation would only be possible after the psychological liberation of individuals, the early 1970s saw pioneering directors such as Med Hondo (b. 1936), from Mauritania and based in Paris, go beyond simply imitating Western films to arrive at a cinema with a distinctly African voice that addressed the issues affecting its people.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In East Africa, Mirt sost shi amit (Harvest: 3,000 Years, 1976) by Ethiopian Haile Gerima (b. 1946) was a landmark, a furious and formally radical denunciation of the oppression suffered by Ethiopia's peasants at the hands of landowners, with characters who symbolized the relationship between Africa and the West. At the same time, in North Africa, filmmakers such as Tunisian Abdellatif Ben Ammar (b. 1943) were also producing challenging films, such as the award-winning Aziza (1980). Chronique des années de braise (Chronicle of the Years of Fire, 1975), by Mohammed Lakhdar Hamina (b. 1934), portrayed Algeria's struggle to free itself from French colonial rule. The film created a new awareness of Algerian cinema, winning the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival.

segments.original: If Western and Asian cinema have their roots in literature and theater, African directors found inspiration by looking to the African tradition of oral storytelling. Films such as Hondo's documentary Soleil O (1973), about immigrants in France, and Emitaï (1971), about the conflict between the French army and Senegalese villagers at the end of World War II, employed key devices of that tradition, such as flashbacks and out-of-sequence narratives.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Following in the footsteps of Sembene and Hondo, directors emerged from all over sub-Saharan Africa, people like Ababacar Samb-Makharam (1934-1987), director of Kodou (1970), or Safi Faye (b. 1943), also from Senegal, who became the first woman film director in sub-Saharan Africa with the feature Kaddu Beykat (Letter from My Village, 1975), a docufiction told through a letter narrated by Faye herself. The film is set in the village where Faye was born in Senegal and focuses on the daily life and customs of its inhabitants, while also telling the story of a young couple who want to marry but cannot - because a drought has ruined his crops, the man cannot pay his bride's dowry. With independence still recent and postcolonial governments across Africa sinking into corruption, the focus of 1970s African cinema tended to remain on the present.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The films of this period covered a range of controversial and topical subjects. Sembène's Xala (1975) was cut by Senegalese censors because of its scathing commentary on the new post-independence elites, who had simply replaced the abuses of the colonial rulers with abuses of their own. The ambitious Ceddo (1977), although set in the 19th century, had a clear message to convey about contemporary Africa by telling the story of African traditions under threat from outside forces.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The lyrical Muna Moto (1975), by Jean-Pierre Dikongué-Pipa (b. 1940) of Cameroon, followed Kaddu Beykat in criticizing the system of putting a price on brides. And an important new voice emerged with director Souleymane Cissé (b. 1940) of Mali, who, like Sembène, had studied in Moscow. Cissé's second feature, Baara (Work, 1978), explored the daily lives of workers at a textile factory in Bamako and revealed Cissé's Marxist background in its portrayal of an engineer who challenges the factory owners. The film won the top prize at Fespaco, as did his next one, Finyé (The Wind, 1982), which dealt with class and generational conflict and showed students who dared to challenge the authority of the military government.

segments.speaker: citacao
segments.original: I argue that Xala evokes two problematic binary oppositions: between the corruption and decadence of foreign influence and the purity and morality of African tradition, the former represented as 'corrupt' and the latter as 'redemptive'; and between strong, revolutionary 'masculine' women and 'feminine' men: villains and weaklings.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: If contemporary reality and its themes dominated African cinema in the 1970s, the following decade saw its directors turn their gaze to the precolonial past in search of inspiration. This shift gave rise to a slower-paced cinema, rooted more specifically in African myths than in the furious statements of the previous decade. The conditions for this came from Burkina Faso, a small West African country. As host of the Fespaco festival, it had already had an impact on African cinema out of all proportion to its status as one of the poorest nations on the continent.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: However, in the early 1980s, with the support of the nation's young and charismatic leader, Thomas Sankara, the country began producing films that had a crucial influence on the development of African cinema. Wend Kuuni (God's Gift, 1982), by Gaston Kaboré (b. 1951), was the great landmark. Set in the precolonial era, it revolves around a mute boy found alone in the bush and adopted by villagers. Kaboré's next film, Zan Boko (1988), implicitly criticized the political situation in Burkina Faso at the time. Kaboré inspired other directors, among them his fellow countryman Idrissa Ouedraogo (b. 1951), who made his own "village" films, including the acclaimed Yaaba (1989), in which a 10-year-old boy befriends an elderly woman who has become an outcast.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The most celebrated African film of the 1980s also follows the example of Wend Kuuni. With the extraordinary Yeelen (1987), Souleymane Cissé left behind the contemporary realism of Baara and Finyé and told a story of myth, magic and ritual set in 11th-century Mali, based on tales passed down through oral tradition. The film has some of the most beautiful cinematography in world cinema. Other notable African films of the period include Med Hondo's epic Sarraounia (1986). In this historical drama, Hondo immortalized one of the few African tribal leaders to oppose French expansionism - Sarraounia, of the Azna - who in 1899 fought the better-equipped colonial military forces with guerrilla tactics.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Hondo's film was acclaimed by critics and won the top prize at Fespaco. The 1980s also saw the arrival of a new generation from sub-Saharan Africa, among them the great Malian director Cheick Oumar Sissoko (b. 1945), whose first feature, Nyamanton (The Garbage Boys, 1986), portrays the lives of street children in Bamako. In Burkina Faso, S. Pierre Yaméogo (b. 1955) also emerged as a name to watch.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: These talents ensured that African cinema remained a vital presence on the international scene during the 1990s, a period that also saw the flourishing of a direct-to-video film industry in the former British colonies of Ghana and Nigeria - countries where cinema had until then been hampered by a lack of financial and structural support similar to what France had offered its former colonies.
